-The cosmic microwave background radiation --- the thermal afterglow of the hot, dense early Universe --- encodes detailed information about the matter content of the cosmos.
-The temperature anisotropy power spectrum, measured with high precision by the Planck satellite, encodes the physics of acoustic oscillations in the primordial baryon-photon plasma before recombination~\cite{Aghanim:2018eyx,Cirelli:2024ssz}.
-Baryons load the oscillating fluid, enhancing the compressional (odd-numbered) acoustic peaks relative to the rarefaction (even-numbered) ones; the ratio of the first to the second peak therefore directly constrains the physical baryon density~\cite{Cirelli:2024ssz}.
-Dark matter, on the other hand, does not couple to the photon pressure and instead provides the gravitational scaffolding within which the oscillations occur.

currentVersionContext:
+The cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation is the thermal relic of the hot, dense early Universe.
+Roughly 380,000 years after the Big Bang, the expanding cosmos cooled sufficiently for protons and electrons to combine into neutral hydrogen --- an epoch known as \emph{recombination}.
+Before this transition, baryonic matter existed as a hot plasma tightly coupled to photons through Thomson scattering; after recombination, photons streamed freely, and this ``last scattering surface'' is what we observe today as the CMB.
+Its temperature is remarkably uniform at ${\sim}\,2.725$~K, but carries tiny anisotropies at the level of ${\sim}\,10^{-5}$ that encode a wealth of information about the matter-energy content of the cosmos.
+
+These anisotropies are conventionally decomposed into angular scales via the temperature power spectrum $C_\ell$.
+Peaks in $C_\ell$ correspond to sound waves in the pre-recombination baryon-photon plasma that were caught at maximum compression or rarefaction at the moment of decoupling; the positions and heights of these peaks encode the composition and geometry of the Universe~\cite{Aghanim:2018eyx,Cirelli:2024ssz}.
+Baryons load the oscillating fluid, enhancing the compressional (odd-numbered) peaks relative to the rarefaction (even-numbered) ones, so that the ratio of the first to the second peak directly constrains the physical baryon density.
+Dark matter, which does not couple to the photon pressure, provides the gravitational scaffolding within which the oscillations occur: its abundance sets the overall depth of the potential wells and modulates the relative heights of successive peaks --- in particular, a universe without cold dark matter would produce a strongly suppressed third peak, in clear contradiction with the observed spectrum~\cite{Cirelli:2024ssz}.

-The final, logically essential element is Big Bang Nucleosynthesis.
-The production of light elements during the first few minutes after the Big Bang is exquisitely sensitive to the baryon-to-photon ratio.
-Measured primordial abundances of deuterium, $^4$He, and $^7$Li tightly constrain the baryon density to $\Omega_b h^2 \approx 0.022$~\cite{Cirelli:2024ssz}, in excellent agreement with the independent CMB determination.
-Since the total matter density is $\Omega_m h^2 \approx 0.14$ --- nearly seven times larger --- the majority of the matter in the Universe cannot be made of baryons~\cite{Cirelli:2024ssz}.
-This is the logical bridge: the astrophysical evidence reviewed in this section demonstrates that dark matter exists; BBN proves that it is not composed of ordinary atoms.
-Whatever dark matter is, it must be a new form of matter beyond the Standard Model --- a conclusion that motivates the particle physics discussion of the following section.
currentVersionContext:
+A crucial independent constraint comes from Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN).
+The production of light elements during the first few minutes after the Big Bang is exquisitely sensitive to the baryon-to-photon ratio: the primordial abundances of deuterium, $^4$He, and $^7$Li tightly constrain the baryon density to $\Omega_b h^2 \approx 0.022$~\cite{Iocco:2008va,ParticleDataGroup:2022pth}, in excellent agreement with the independent CMB determination.
+Since the total matter density inferred from the dynamics and lensing reviewed above is $\Omega_m h^2 \approx 0.14$ --- nearly seven times larger --- the majority of the matter in the Universe cannot be made of baryons.
+One might ask whether this missing matter could simply be a form of ordinary matter that happens to be dark: cold molecular gas clouds, compact stellar remnants, or some as-yet-undetected baryonic component hiding in the intergalactic medium.
+BBN decisively rules out this possibility.
+The light-element abundances constrain the \emph{total} baryon density, not just the visible fraction; any baryonic matter, however dark or diffuse, would have participated in nucleosynthesis during the first few minutes and altered the primordial element yields.
+The observed abundances of deuterium and helium are consistent with $\Omega_b h^2 \approx 0.022$ and leave no room for a hidden baryonic reservoir.
+Whatever dark matter is, it must therefore be \emph{non-baryonic} --- a new form of matter beyond the Standard Model --- a conclusion that motivates the particle physics discussion of the following section.
